subject: Clement of Alexandria

text_used.text: Every quotation of Clement below is checked word for word (case-insensitive, footnote numbers removed, whitespace collapsed) against William Wilson's translation in the Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (American edition, ed. A. Cleveland Coxe, 1885), downloaded whole from CCEL as plain text and split per work under sources/people/clement-of-alexandria/anf02-*.txt. 'exact' is the translation as printed. 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God. Eusebius is McGiffert's translation (NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890), Jerome is Richardson (Lives of Illustrious Men, NPNF2 vol. 3) and Fremantle (Letter 70, NPNF2 vol. 6), all from CCEL plain text. Every chapter link below was fetched (HTTP 200) and the line was found on that very page.
text_used.source: Philip Schaff (ed.), ANF02: Fathers of the Second Century, CCEL plain text, marked 'Rights: Public Domain'
text_used.note: New Advent's copy (newadvent.org/fathers/0207.htm, 02091-02108.htm, 020801-020812.htm) is the same translation 'revised and edited' by Kevin Knight: it modernises thee/thou/thy to you/your and in a few places restores words. Two of the quiz's shown lines use New Advent's modernised wording (see where_he_stood and site_data_flags). CCEL's chapter pages are numbered by page, not by chapter: e.g. Stromata Book 4, chapter 10 is the page anf02.vi.iv.iv.ix, and chapters 23 to 26 of Book 4 share one page. The URLs below are the pages the lines were actually found on.

born.text: About 150, probably at Athens. Even in the 4th century there were two traditions: Athens or Alexandria.
born.source: Wace, Dictionary of Christian Biography (1911), 'Clement of Alexandria' (B. F. Westcott): Epiphanius (Panarion 32.6) says 'some saying that he was an Alexandrian, others that he was an Athenian'; Westcott concludes 'an Athenian by training if not by origin' and dates his birth 'c. a.d. 150-160'. Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): 'Athens is given as the starting-point of his journeyings, and was probably his birthplace.' Britannica: 'born 150 ce, Athens'. Benedict XVI, General Audience 18 April 2007: 'probably born in Athens at around the middle of the second century'.
born.note: Epiphanius is read through Westcott's quotation (Greek given there: 'ὅν φασί τινες Ἀλεξανδρέα ἕτεροι δὲ Ἀθηναῖον'). I did not fetch the Panarion itself; its only full English version (Williams) is in copyright. copticchurch.net says the same: 'two traditions in the time of St. Epiphanius (in the fourth century), giving Athens or Alexandria'. Plain wording that holds: 'Born about 150, probably at Athens.'

grew_up.text: Nothing is recorded of his parents. He became a Christian by his own choice, as an adult. He had a broad Greek education and knew the pagan poets and philosophers well.
grew_up.source: Wace DCB (Westcott): 'Nothing is recorded of his parentage; but his own language seems to imply that he embraced Christianity by a personal act'; McGiffert, note to Eusebius, Church History 5.11: 'He received a very extensive education, and became a Christian in adult years'; Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): 'He became a convert to the Faith'
grew_up.note: Britannica says 'to pagan parents' and copticchurch.net says 'His parents were not Christians', but Westcott says whether they were Christian or pagan is not known. Do not print 'pagan parents' as fact. His full name, Titus Flavius Clemens, has made some guess at a link to the Flavian family: Westcott calls this unproven.

died.text: Date, place and cause unknown. He was alive about 211, when he carried a letter from Alexander to Antioch. By Alexander's letter to Origen, written about 215, he was dead.
died.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.11 and 6.14; McGiffert's note to 6.14 ('at the time of the writing of this epistle both Pantaenus and Clement were dead'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): 'died about the year 215', 'In another letter written about 215 to Origen Alexander speaks of Clement as of one then dead'; Wace DCB: 'The time and the place of his death are alike unknown'; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022: 'The exact time and place of his death are unknown'; Britannica: 'died between 211 and 215'
died.note: Wikipedia's infobox gives 'Jerusalem' as the place of death with no source. No ancient text says where he died.

buried.text: Unknown. No source records his grave.
buried.source: Wace DCB; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (time and place of death unknown)
buried.note: Leave the 'Buried' row out of the sheet, or print 'Unknown'.

full_name.text: Titus Flavius Clemens. Eusebius gives the title of the Miscellanies as 'Titus Flavius Clement's Stromata of Gnostic Notes on the True Philosophy'.

roles.text: Seeker: studied under six teachers across the Greek world before he 'found rest' with the last, in Egypt.
roles.source: Stromata 1.1; McGiffert's note to Church History 5.11 ('names six different teachers'); Wace DCB ('six illustrious teachers')
roles.note: Short line for the path: 'Six teachers, then Egypt'.

roles.text: Teacher: pupil, then successor, of Pantaenus at the head of the catechetical school of Alexandria, from about 190.
roles.source: Eusebius, Church History 5.11 and 6.6; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 38; Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): 'Clement first assisted and then succeeded Pantaenus in the direction of the school, about A.D. 190'
roles.note: Britannica says 'around 180'; the Catholic Encyclopedia, Westcott and the Episcopal Church say about 190. Use 'about 190'.

roles.text: Presbyter (priest) of the church of Alexandria. Never a bishop.
roles.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 38 ('presbyter of the Alexandrian church'); Alexander of Jerusalem in Eusebius 6.11 ('the blessed presbyter'); McGiffert's note to 5.11: 'He was never a bishop, but was a presbyter of the Alexandrian church'

roles.text: Writer: the Exhortation to the Greeks, the Instructor and the Miscellanies (Stromata), plus Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
Exile and helper: left Alexandria in the persecution of 202; later strengthened the church of his old pupil Alexander, who was in prison for the faith, about 211.
roles.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.3 and 6.11; Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), after Duchesne
roles.note: Eusebius never says in so many words that Clement fled; that he left in 202 is the historians' inference (McGiffert's note to 6.6; Wace DCB; Catholic Encyclopedia). Word it as 'left'.

also_called.text: Titus Flavius Clemens; in Latin Clemens Alexandrinus.
also_called.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.13; CCEL's heading to Who Is the Rich Man ('Clemens Alexandrinus')

also_called.text: 'Clement the Stromateus' (the Miscellanist): Cassiodorus writes 'Clemens Alexandrinus presbyter, qui et Stromateus vocatur'.
also_called.source: Cassiodorus, Institutions 1.8, as quoted by Pope Benedict XIV, Postquam intelleximus (1748), section 28, printed in the Roman Martyrology of 1749
also_called.note: Read in the archive.org OCR text of the 1749 Martyrology (OCR reads 'vocatur, id est' cleanly). I did not open Cassiodorus directly.

also_called.text: 'Clement of Alexandria, Priest and Theologian' (Episcopal Church). 'Clement of Alexandria, Priest and Teacher of the Faith' (ACNA).
also_called.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; ACNA Book of Common Prayer 2019, calendar

also_called.text: 'St. Clement' in the Coptic Church's own writing, and in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908).
also_called.source: copticchurch.net, 'The School of Alexandria Before Origen', Part IV ('The Life of St. Clement'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): 'St. Clement was an early Greek theologian'
also_called.note: The Coptic book is Fr Tadros Y. Malaty's (the page does not name him; it is the well-known source of this series). Benedict XVI's 2007 catechesis calls him simply 'Clement of Alexandria' while calling the Father before him 'St Irenaeus'.

status.text: Church Father. Honoured on Anglican calendars (the Episcopal Church, ACNA and the Anglican Church of Canada, on 5 December) and called 'St Clement' by Coptic writers. Not on the Catholic, Orthodox or Coptic calendars.
status.note: Status line corrected by the checker: 'Kept by some Anglican churches' (the Church of England does not keep him; the Episcopal Church, ACNA and the Anglican Church of Canada do, on 5 December, and Canada's 1962 BCP on 4 December).

patron_of.text: No patronage found in any source checked.
patron_of.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), Wace DCB, Britannica, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022: none names one
patron_of.note: Leave 'Patron of' out of the sheet.

in_art.text: No fixed attribute. Artists imagined him: André Thevet's 1584 engraving shows an old bearded scholar seated in a chair, pointing as he speaks. Ingres's 1842 design for a window in the Chapelle Saint-Ferdinand, Paris, shows him haloed, arms raised in prayer, and labels him 'S. CLEMENS ALEXANDRINVS EPISCOPVS', a bishop, which he never was.
in_art.source: The pictures themselves (Commons files below); Louvre record INV 20314, 'Saint Clément, évêque d'Alexandrie' (1842): 'le saint debout sur un podium de face les mains levées en prière'
in_art.note: No likeness survives from his lifetime. Every picture is imagined.

wrote.text: Surviving: the Exhortation to the Greeks (Protrepticus), the Instructor (Paedagogus, 3 books), the Miscellanies (Stromata, 7 books, plus a so-called 8th of notes), and Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? Lost but for fragments: the Outlines (Hypotyposes) and others. Eusebius lists ten works.
wrote.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.13 (the list); McGiffert's note 1840 ('Eusebius names ten works in this chapter'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): the Miscellanies 'comprise seven entire books'; the eighth 'is nothing more than a collection of extracts'
wrote.note: Also surviving in fragments: Excerpts from Theodotus and the Prophetic Eclogues (Catholic Encyclopedia). The ANF gives Stromata Book 3 wholly in Latin: 'After much consideration, the Editors have deemed it best to give the whole of this book in Latin' (ANF note 2440), because it deals with sexual ethics and the libertine sects; Instructor Book 2, chapter 10 is also left in Latin.

pronounced.note: Merriam-Webster's 'Clement of Alexandria' biography entry exists but gives no pronunciation on the page; the two parts are taken from its 'Clement' and 'Alexandria' entries.

west.text: None. He is not in the General Roman Calendar or the Roman Martyrology. The 1916 English Roman Martyrology has no Clement of Alexandria on 4 December.
west.source: The Roman Martyrology (1916), 4 December (Peter Chrysologus, Barbara, Meletius, Osmund and others; no Clement); Benedict XIV, Postquam intelleximus (1748), sections 19 to 31
west.note: I did not check the current (2004) Martyrology. Before the Roman Martyrology of the 1580s, the Martyrology of Usuard (9th century) had a 'St Clement' on 4 December, which Clement's defenders took to be him (Benedict XIV, section 22). Catholic Encyclopedia: 'his feast fell on the fourth of December'.

west.church: Anglican Church of Canada (Book of Common Prayer, 1962)
west.source: Anglican Church of Canada, The Book of Common Prayer (1962), calendar, p. xii (December), PDF on anglican.ca
west.note: ADDED BY THE CHECKER, 2026-09-25. The draft said no church keeps 4 December now; the Canadian 1962 BCP does (fetched text: sources/people/clement-of-alexandria/anglican-church-of-canada-bcp1962-calendar.txt). Its newer Book of Alternative Services keeps 5 December.

west.text: 'Clement of Alexandria, Priest and Theologian, c. 210'.
west.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, calendar and pp. 548-549 (page footer 'December 5')
west.note: The PDF's calendar page, run through pdftotext, prints '4' beside his name because the day numbers slip a line; the propers page footer says 'December 5', and the calendar order (John of Damascus 4, Clement 5, Nicholas 6, Ambrose 7) confirms 5 December.

west.text: 'Clement of Alexandria, Priest and Teacher of the Faith, 210'.
west.source: The Book of Common Prayer (2019), ACNA, calendar, December

west.text: 'Dec. 5: Clement of Alexandria' (Book of Alternative Services dates).
west.source: Anglican Church of Canada, 'Advent' church-year page

west.text: Not kept. Common Worship has Clement of Rome on 23 November, and nothing for Clement of Alexandria in December (1 Charles de Foucauld, 3 Francis Xavier, 4 John of Damascus and Nicholas Ferrar, 6 Nicholas, 7 Ambrose).
west.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar

west.text: Not kept. The LCMS list has Clement of Rome (23 November) and John of Damascus (4 December), no Clement of Alexandria. The ELCA's Evangelical Lutheran Worship calendar likewise has Clement of Rome only.
west.source: LCMS, 'Commemorations' page; Evangelical Lutheran Worship church year (2006 draft PDF, archived)

east.text: None. He is not on the Orthodox calendar. The Greek synaxarion keeps Clement of Rome on 24 November, not him.
east.source: OrthodoxWiki, 'Clement of Alexandria': 'Clement is not commemorated as a saint in Eastern Orthodoxy'; saint.gr (Orthodox Synaxaristis): Clement of Rome 'Εορτάζει στις 24 Νοεμβρίου'
east.note: OrthodoxWiki is a wiki, not a church calendar. A search of saint.gr's synaxarion through a web search turned up Clement of Rome, Clement of Ohrid and Clement of Ancyra, but no Clement of Alexandria. OCA and GOARCH were not checked directly (absence is hard to prove on their sites).

east.text: No day in the Synaxarium. The Coptic Church's own site calls him 'St. Clement', and a Coptic school is named after him (per Wikipedia), but its Synaxarium lists only Clement of Rome (Hatour 29) and Clement of Ancyra (Toba 28).
east.source: copticchurch.net Synaxarium, full English index ('The Martyrdom of St. Clement, Pope of Rome', Hator 29; 'The Martyrdom of St. Clement', Toba 28, whose entry is the martyr of Angora/Ancyra under Diocletian)
east.note: Wikipedia says the Coptic Church venerates him and gives 4 December 'Eastern Catholicism, Anglicanism'; neither is backed by a church calendar I could find. The Coptic calendar is not the only possible source (some Coptic churches may keep him locally); say 'not in the Synaxarium'.

feast_days.note: Why so few dates? The old Western martyrologies kept a St Clement on 4 December. When the Roman Martyrology was drawn up in the 1580s, Cardinal Baronius did not carry the name over, and in 1748 Pope Benedict XIV refused to add it (see is_he_a_saint). The Anglican churches that added him in the 20th century use 5 December. No source I found says why 5 rather than 4.

numbers.text: He names six teachers he studied under, from Greece, southern Italy and the East, until he found the last one hidden in Egypt.
numbers.source: Stromata 1.1; McGiffert's note to Church History 5.11 ('names six different teachers under whom he studied Christianity'); Wace DCB ('He enumerates six illustrious teachers')
numbers.note: Clement's own sentence is hard to count (an Ionian in Greece, one in Magna Graecia, one from Coele-Syria, one from Egypt, an Assyrian, a Hebrew, then 'the last'). Six is the count of McGiffert and Westcott; print it as theirs if space allows.

numbers.text: He led the school at Alexandria from about 190 until he left in the persecution of 202: about twelve years.
numbers.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): succeeded Pantaenus 'about A.D. 190'; McGiffert's note to 5.11: head of the school 'probably until 202'; Wace DCB: 'c. a.d. 190-203'
numbers.note: An approximate number built from two approximate dates. Print 'About 12'. Britannica's 'around 180' start would make it about 22; say 'about'.

numbers.text: Eusebius knew all eight books of the Stromata. Seven survive whole; what is called the eighth is a set of notes.
numbers.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.13 ('All the eight Stromata of Clement are preserved among us'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1908)

numbers.text: Eusebius names ten works by Clement.
numbers.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.13; McGiffert's note 1840: 'Eusebius names ten works in this chapter'
numbers.note: The four whole: Exhortation, Instructor, Stromata (7 books), Rich Man.

traits.title: a seeker
traits.text: He went from teacher to teacher, in Greece, in southern Italy and in the East. Only when he tracked down the last, hidden in Egypt, did he stop.
traits.exact: When I came upon the last (he was the first in power), having tracked him out concealed in Egypt, I found rest.
traits.display: When I came upon the last (he was the first in power), having tracked him out concealed in Egypt, I found rest.
traits.note: The last teacher is Pantaenus, as Eusebius (5.11) and the ANF footnote take it. Clement calls him 'the true, the Sicilian bee'.

traits.title: took truth wherever he found it
traits.text: He would not follow one school of philosophy. He took what each said well, and he mocked Christians who feared Greek learning.
traits.exact: But the multitude are frightened at the Hellenic philosophy, as children are at masks, being afraid lest it lead them astray.
traits.display: But the multitude are frightened at the Hellenic philosophy, as children are at masks, being afraid lest it lead them astray.
traits.note: Pair with Stromata 1.7: 'whatever has been well said by each of those sects ... this eclectic whole I call philosophy.'

traits.title: grave and cheerful
traits.text: His rule book goes down to laughter, eating and sleep. A pleasant word is fine, he says, but not clowning.
traits.exact: For man is not to laugh on all occasions because he is a laughing animal, any more than the horse neighs on all occasions because he is a neighing animal.
traits.display: For man is not to laugh on all occasions because he is a laughing animal, any more than the horse neighs on all occasions because he is a neighing animal.
traits.note: His ideal Christian is 'at once grave and cheerful in all things' (Stromata 7.7). Same chapter: 'Pleasantry is allowable, not waggery.'

traits.title: gentle with the rich
traits.text: He called those who flatter the rich 'godless and treacherous'. Then he spent a whole sermon telling rich believers they could be saved, if they gave up greed, not money.
traits.exact: So let no man destroy wealth, rather than the passions of the soul, which are incompatible with the better use of wealth.
traits.display: So let no man destroy wealth, rather than the passions of the soul, which are incompatible with the better use of wealth.
traits.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
traits.note: 'flatterers and base ... but also godless and treacherous': section 1. On giving: 'Do not you judge who is worthy or who is unworthy' (section 33).

others_on_him.exact: I have sent this letter to you by Clement, the blessed presbyter, a man virtuous and approved, whom ye yourselves also know and will recognize. Being here, in the providence and oversight of the Master, he has strengthened and built up the Church of the Lord.
others_on_him.who: Alexander, then a bishop in prison for the faith, later bishop of Jerusalem, writing to the church of Antioch about 211
others_on_him.note: Tr. A. C. McGiffert, 1890. Jerome gives the same letter in Lives of Illustrious Men 38.

others_on_him.exact: For we know well those blessed fathers who have trodden the way before us, with whom we shall soon be; Pantænus, the truly blessed man and master, and the holy Clement, my master and benefactor
others_on_him.who: Alexander of Jerusalem, in a letter to Origen, after Clement's death
others_on_him.note: Benedict XIV (1748) cites this 'sanctum Clementem' as the oldest witness that he was called holy.

others_on_him.exact: Clement, a presbyter of Alexandria, in my judgment the most learned of men, wrote eight books of Miscellanies and as many of Outline Sketches, a treatise against the Gentiles, and three volumes called the Pedagogue. Is there any want of learning in these, or are they not rather drawn from the very heart of philosophy?
others_on_him.note: Tr. W. H. Fremantle (NPNF2 vol. 6, 1893). Section number from the NPNF text's own numbering; show readers 'Letter 70, to Magnus'.

life_moments.title: Six teachers, then rest
life_moments.text: As a young man he travelled in search of teachers: an Ionian in Greece, others in southern Italy, others in the East, an Assyrian and a Hebrew in Palestine. Then he tracked down the last one, hidden in Egypt, and stayed. He calls him 'the true, the Sicilian bee', gathering from the meadow of the prophets and apostles. This was Pantaenus of Alexandria.
life_moments.source: Stromata, Book 1, chapter 1; Eusebius, Church History 5.11 (identifies Pantaenus)
life_moments.note: Clement names no one; Eusebius says 'It seems to me that he alludes to' Pantaenus. Keep 'This was Pantaenus, says Eusebius'.

life_moments.title: Head of the school
life_moments.text: Alexandria was the ancient world's great city of learning. Its church ran a school where new Christians and curious pagans could hear the faith explained. Clement first helped Pantaenus there, then took his place.
life_moments.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.6 ('Clement having succeeded Pantaenus, had charge at that time of the catechetical instruction in Alexandria'); Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 38; Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): 'Lectures were given to which pagan hearers were admitted'

life_moments.title: A boy called Origen
life_moments.text: Among his pupils was a boy named Origen, who became the most famous Christian thinker of the next generation. Another pupil, Alexander, became bishop of Jerusalem and stayed his friend for life.
life_moments.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.6 ('Origen also, while still a boy, was one of his pupils') and 6.14 (Alexander's letter); Jerome, Lives 38 ('Origen is known to have been his disciple')
life_moments.note: That Alexander was his pupil is inferred from Alexander's letter (McGiffert's note 1879: 'The epistle does not state this directly').

life_moments.title: Three books for three stages
life_moments.text: He wrote an appeal to pagans (the Exhortation), a guide to daily Christian life (the Instructor), and a rambling notebook of deeper teaching (the Miscellanies). He says he planted the Miscellanies on purpose like a wild hillside, mixing fruit trees with barren ones, to hide the fruit from thieves.
life_moments.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1908) on the 'trilogy'; Stromata, Book 7, chapter 18
life_moments.note: Eusebius 6.6: the Stromata's chronology runs to the death of Commodus, 'So it is evident that that work was written during the reign of Severus'.

life_moments.title: Persecution empties the school
life_moments.text: In 202 the emperor Severus's persecution fell on Egypt. Origen's father was killed. Eusebius says there was soon no one left in Alexandria to teach the faith, 'as all were driven away by the threat of persecution'. Clement left the city and, as far as we know, never came back.
life_moments.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.1-6.3; McGiffert's note to 6.6; Wace DCB ('Clement retired from Alexandria ... never, as it seems, to return')
life_moments.note: Eusebius does not name Clement in 6.3; the link is the historians'. McGiffert: 'That it was not unworthy cowardice which led Clement to take his departure is clear enough from the words of Alexander'.

life_moments.title: With a bishop in prison
life_moments.text: His old pupil Alexander was now a bishop in Cappadocia, and in prison for the faith. Clement was with him and looked after his church. When Antioch chose a new bishop, Alexander sent his letter of joy there by Clement's hand, praising him as the man who had 'strengthened and built up the Church of the Lord'.
life_moments.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.11; Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), after Duchesne
life_moments.note: Eusebius: 'Alexander, a servant and prisoner of Jesus Christ'. Dating about 211 from McGiffert and the Catholic Encyclopedia ('211 or 212').

life_moments.title: Gone before
life_moments.text: A few years later Alexander wrote to Origen about 'those blessed fathers who have trodden the way before us', naming 'the holy Clement, my master and benefactor'. Clement had died. No one recorded where or how.

miracles.text: None. No early source records a miracle by Clement or at his grave; his life is known only from his own books, Eusebius, Jerome and Alexander's letters. Leave the miracles section out.
miracles.source: Eusebius, Church History 5.11, 6.6, 6.11, 6.13, 6.14; Jerome, Lives 38; Benedict XIV (1748), section 26: the old writers are silent about his life and way of life
miracles.note: The story Clement tells of the apostle John and the robber (Rich Man, section 42) is a repentance story, not a miracle; it belongs in 'His own words' or a tidbit.

framing.text: Clement wrote a great deal, and his own books survive. These lines are from William Wilson's translation in the Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885).

feature.exact: the Word of God became man, that thou mayest learn from man how man may become God.
feature.display: The Word of God became man, that thou mayest learn from man how man may become God.
feature.context: From his appeal to pagans. It is one of the earliest statements of what the East calls theosis: God became human so that humans might share in God's life.
feature.greek: ὁ λόγος ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος γενόμενος, ἵνα δὴ καὶ σὺ παρὰ ἀνθρώπου μάθῃς, πῇ ποτε ἄρα ἄνθρωπος γένηται θεός.
feature.greek_source: Protrepticus 1 (Butterworth's Loeb Greek text, 1919), Perseus Digital Library
feature.note: ANF titles the work 'Exhortation to the Heathen'. The sentence opens mid-line ('yea, I say, the Word of God became man'). The 'theosis' gloss in the context line is my plain summary; if a source is wanted, Benedict XVI (2007): 'man's ultimate end is to liken himself to God'. Greek checked word for word on the Perseus page (saved as perseus-protrepticus-greek-chapter-1.txt).

lines.exact: Holding festival, then, in our whole life, persuaded that God is altogether on every side present, we cultivate our fields, praising; we sail the sea, hymning; in all the rest of our conversation we conduct ourselves according to rule.
lines.display: Holding festival, then, in our whole life, persuaded that God is altogether on every side present, we cultivate our fields, praising; we sail the sea, hymning; in all the rest of our conversation we conduct ourselves according to rule.
lines.context: His picture of the mature Christian: all of life is a feast day, because God is everywhere.
lines.note: The source of the site's hook 'he called the whole of life a festival'. 'Conversation' here means way of life.

lines.exact: It is then, as appears, the greatest of all lessons to know one's self. For if one knows himself, he will know God; and knowing God, he will be made like God, not by wearing gold or long robes, but by well-doing, and by requiring as few things as possible.
lines.display: It is then, as appears, the greatest of all lessons to know one's self. For if one knows himself, he will know God; and knowing God, he will be made like God, not by wearing gold or long robes, but by well-doing, and by requiring as few things as possible.
lines.context: Opening a chapter on true beauty.
lines.note: A good fit for a self-understanding site.

lines.exact: Some men, in truth, live that they may eat, as the irrational creatures, "whose life is their belly, and nothing else." But the Instructor enjoins us to eat that we may live.
lines.display: Some men, in truth, live that they may eat, as the irrational creatures, “whose life is their belly, and nothing else.” But the Instructor enjoins us to eat that we may live.
lines.context: 'The Instructor' is Christ. The 'eat to live' saying is older (it is credited to Socrates), but this is Clement's own use of it.
lines.note: The Socrates attribution is common knowledge but I did not source it; cut that clause if unsure.

lines.exact: The way of truth is therefore one. But into it, as into a perennial river, streams flow from all sides.
lines.display: The way of truth is therefore one. But into it, as into a perennial river, streams flow from all sides.
lines.context: On why Christians may learn from Greek philosophy.

lines.exact: He hath changed sunset into sunrise, and through the cross brought death to life
lines.display: He hath changed sunset into sunrise, and through the cross brought death to life
lines.context: Of Christ, the 'Sun of Righteousness'. A 1939 hymn, 'Sunset to sunrise changes now', grew from this line.
lines.note: The line continues with a semicolon; end the display with a full stop or an ellipsis. The link to the hymn is from Hymnary.org's credit (author Clement, paraphraser Howard Chandler Robbins, 1939).

lines.exact: Why, my son, dost thou flee from me, thy father, unarmed, old? Son, pity me. Fear not; thou hast still hope of life. I will give account to Christ for thee.
lines.display: Why, my son, dost thou flee from me, thy father, unarmed, old? Son, pity me. Fear not; thou hast still hope of life. I will give account to Christ for thee.
lines.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
lines.context: Clement's story of the old apostle John chasing a young bandit chief on horseback, to bring him back to Christ. He tells it as 'a tale, which is not a tale but a narrative'.
lines.note: These are John's words in Clement's story, not Clement's own. Label them so. The youth 'baptized a second time with tears'. Eusebius copies the whole story (Church History 3.23).

lines.exact: Do not you judge who is worthy or who is unworthy. For it is possible you may be mistaken in your opinion.
lines.display: Do not you judge who is worthy or who is unworthy. For it is possible you may be mistaken in your opinion.

lines.context: On giving to the poor. He goes on: better to help the undeserving too than to miss the deserving.

more_if_needed.exact: His whole life is prayer and converse with God.
more_if_needed.note: 'His' is the mature Christian, not God.

more_if_needed.exact: Sleepless light is now over all, and the west has given credence to the east.
He has gathered the bloodless host of peace, and assigned to them the kingdom of heaven.
thus custom pleases and tickles; but custom pushes into the abyss, while truth conducts to heaven.
more_if_needed.note: Answer to pagans who said it was wrong to leave their fathers' customs.

more_if_needed.exact: it is possible for the man who formerly led a bad and dissolute life, on afterwards repenting, to overcome in the time after repentance the evil conduct of a long time.

more_if_needed.exact: one is not really shown to be a man in the choice of single life; but he surpasses men, who, disciplined by marriage, procreation of children, and care for the house, without pleasure or pain, in his solicitude for the house has been inseparable from God's love
more_if_needed.note: Unusual among the Fathers: marriage as the harder test.

more_if_needed.note: Women and men, slave and free. The same chapter keeps distinct roles.

The Gnostic, then, is very closely allied to God, being at once grave and cheerful in all things,--grave on account of the bent of his soul towards the Divinity, and cheerful on account of his consideration of the blessings of humanity which God hath given us.
more_if_needed.note: 'The Gnostic' is his word for the mature Christian, not the heretical Gnostics he fought.

tidbit_gospels.text: Clement passed on 'the tradition of the earliest presbyters' about the order of the Gospels: those with the genealogies (Matthew and Luke) were written first; Mark wrote down Peter's preaching at Rome at his hearers' request; and 'last of all, John ... composed a spiritual Gospel'.
tidbit_gospels.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.14, from Clement's lost Outlines (Hypotyposes)
tidbit_gospels.note: '(Matthew and Luke)' is my gloss on 'the Gospels containing the genealogies'.

prayer_he_wrote.exact: Be gracious, O Instructor, to us Thy children, Father, Charioteer of Israel, Son and Father, both in One, O Lord. Grant to us who obey Thy precepts, that we may perfect the likeness of the image, and with all our power know Him who is the good God and not a harsh judge. And do Thou Thyself cause that all of us who have our conversation in Thy peace, who have been translated into Thy commonwealth, having sailed tranquilly over the billows of sin, may be wafted in calm by Thy Holy Spirit, by the ineffable wisdom, by night and day to the perfect day; and giving thanks may praise, and praising thank the Alone Father and Son, Son and Father, the Son, Instructor and Teacher, with the Holy Spirit, all in One, in whom is all, for whom all is One, for whom is eternity, whose members we all are, whose glory the æons are; for the All-good, All-lovely, All-wise, All-just One. To whom be glory both now and for ever. Amen.
prayer_he_wrote.display: Be gracious, O Instructor, to us Thy children, Father, Charioteer of Israel, Son and Father, both in One, O Lord. Grant to us who obey Thy precepts, that we may perfect the likeness of the image, and with all our power know Him Who is the good God and not a harsh judge. And do Thou Thyself cause that all of us who have our conversation in Thy peace, who have been translated into Thy commonwealth, having sailed tranquilly over the billows of sin, may be wafted in calm by Thy Holy Spirit, by the ineffable wisdom, by night and day to the perfect day; and giving thanks may praise, and praising thank the Alone Father and Son, Son and Father, the Son, Instructor and Teacher, with the Holy Spirit, all in One, in Whom is all, for Whom all is One, for Whom is eternity, Whose members we all are, Whose glory the æons are; for the All-good, All-lovely, All-wise, All-just One. To Whom be glory both now and for ever. Amen.
prayer_he_wrote.note: Clement's own prayer closing the Instructor, addressed to Christ. A shorter cut for the page: the first two sentences. Right after it comes 'A Hymn to Christ the Saviour' ('Bridle of colts untamed'), headed 'Composed by St. Clement' in the ANF; the Catholic Encyclopedia says the manuscripts attribute it to Clement and it 'may be the work of Clement (Bardenhewer)', or 'of as early a date as the Gloria in Excelsis (Westcott)'. The ANF's English hymn is a rhymed expansion: 'He has been obliged, however, to add somewhat to it' (note 1788). Quote the prayer, not the hymn, as surely his. Careful readers may notice 'Son and Father, both in One': the Catholic Encyclopedia notes he 'seem[s] to approach Modalism' in places.

hard_topics.title: Photius's charges
hard_topics.text: In the 9th century Patriarch Photius read Clement's Outlines (now lost) and listed errors: matter without beginning, the Son 'reduced' to a creature, souls passing from body to body, worlds before Adam, and a Word that only seemed to take flesh. He added that the Instructor was 'entirely free from idle and blasphemous opinions', and that the errors might be someone else's 'under his name'.
exact: Although in some cases what he says appears orthodox, in others he indulges in impious and legendary fables.
He talks much other blasphemous nonsense, either he or some one else under his name.
These discourses have nothing in common with the Outlines, since they are entirely free from idle and blasphemous opinions.
hard_topics.source: Photius, Bibliotheca, codices 109-111, tr. J. H. Freese (1920)
hard_topics.note: Freese 1920 is public domain in the US (published before 1930). The Catholic Encyclopedia answers for his defenders: 'Conservative scholars are inclined to believe that Photius has thrown the mistakes of Clement ... into undue relief.'

hard_topics.title: Did Christ need to eat?
hard_topics.text: Clement wrote that Jesus ate not because His body needed food, but so His companions would not think Him a phantom, and that He felt neither pleasure nor pain. Critics call this close to Docetism; the Catholic Encyclopedia says he 'clearly admits in Christ a real body'.
exact: For He ate, not for the sake of the body, which was kept together by a holy energy, but in order that it might not enter into the minds of those who were with Him to entertain a different opinion of Him
But He was entirely impassible (apathes); inaccessible to any movement of feeling--either pleasure or pain.
hard_topics.note: OrthodoxWiki quotes the same passage in another translation as proof he 'denies Christ's full humanity'. Give both views.

hard_topics.title: Free of all feeling
hard_topics.text: His ideal Christian is never angry and needs no cheerfulness, 'being persuaded that all things happen well'. The Catholic Encyclopedia says this is 'undoubtedly colored by Stoicism': 'the ideal Stoic who has deadened his feelings altogether'.
exact: Nor does he need cheerfulness of mind; for he does not fall into pain, being persuaded that all things happen well.
He is really describing not so much the Christian with his sensitive feelings and desires under due control, but the ideal Stoic who has deadened his feelings altogether.

hard_topics.title: Books 'not received'
hard_topics.text: The Gelasian Decree (6th century, attributed to Pope Gelasius) lists Clement's works among books not to be received. Cassiodorus had his notes on the Catholic Epistles translated into Latin with 'certain stumbling blocks' cut out.
exact: they are in no case to be received amongst us
hard_topics.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1908); Cassiodorus, Institutions 1.8, quoted by Benedict XIV (1748), section 28 ('exclusis quibusdam offendiculis')
hard_topics.note: The CE's own words: a Latin fragment 'translated by Cassiodorus and purged of objectionable passages'.

hard_topics.title: Against rushing to martyrdom, and leaving in 202
hard_topics.text: He taught that Christians should flee persecution, and that anyone who gives himself up shares the guilt of his own death. He left Alexandria when persecution came. McGiffert, Eusebius's editor, defends him: 'it was not unworthy cowardice', as Alexander's praise shows.
exact: If he who kills a man of God sins against God, he also who presents himself before the judgment-seat becomes guilty of his death. And such is also the case with him who does not avoid persecution, but out of daring presents himself for capture.
hard_topics.source: Stromata, Book 4, chapter 10; McGiffert's note to Church History 6.6
hard_topics.note: CCEL page anf02.vi.iv.iv.ix is headed 'Chapter X'.

hard_topics.title: Rules for women
hard_topics.text: His rule book has strict rules on dress, and more for women: 'Let her be entirely covered, unless she happen to be at home.' Yet he also taught that women and men have 'one and the same virtue'.
exact: Let her be entirely covered, unless she happen to be at home.
since it is a fit consequence that the same nature possesses one and the same virtue.
hard_topics.source: The Instructor, Book 3, chapter 11; Stromata, Book 4, chapter 8

hard_topics.title: A hope for the dead who never heard
hard_topics.text: He held that the gospel was preached in Hades, and that God's punishments are meant to heal: 'saving and disciplinary, leading to conversion'. Some modern writers count him an early universalist; in the texts checked he does not say that all will be saved.
exact: since God's punishments are saving and disciplinary, leading to conversion
hard_topics.note: Wikipedia (citing Ramelli, Hart and others) calls him 'one of the first Christian universalists'. The quiz already hides his cell on 'In the end, God will save everyone' (all: v 1, hide true).

hard_topics.title: Allegory everywhere
hard_topics.text: The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'He was ready to find allegory everywhere. The facts of the Old Testament became mere symbols to him.'
exact: He was ready to find allegory everywhere.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: His feast days are 23 November in the West and 24 November in the East.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Those are the days of a different man, Clement of Rome. Britannica prints them for Clement of Alexandria. The Church of England and the 1916 Roman Martyrology keep Clement of Rome on 23 November; the Greek synaxarion keeps him on 24 November.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Britannica, 'Saint Clement of Alexandria' ('Western feast day November 23; Eastern feast day November 24'); Common Worship calendar ('23 Clement, Bishop of Rome, Martyr, c.100'); Roman Martyrology (1916), 23 November ('The birthday of pope St. Clement'); saint.gr, Clement of Rome, 24 November
misquoted_or_legend.note: The one day ever kept for him in the old West is 4 December; Anglicans today keep 5 December.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Pope Sixtus V removed him from the Roman Martyrology in 1586.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: No source I found names Sixtus V. Pope Benedict XIV says Cardinal Baronius, compiling the Roman Martyrology, simply did not carry Clement's name over from the older Martyrology of Usuard. The Catholic Encyclopedia says his name was dropped when the Martyrology 'was revised by Pope Clement VIII'. In 1748 Benedict XIV looked at the case again and refused to add him.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Wikipedia, 'Clement of Alexandria' (the 1586 / Sixtus V sentence is tagged 'citation needed'); Benedict XIV, Postquam intelleximus (1748), section 22: 'Cardinalis Baronius, qui Clementis nomen, quod in Usuardi Martyrologio perlegerat, in Romanum Martyrologium non transtulit'; Catholic Encyclopedia (1908)
misquoted_or_legend.note: Baronius's annotated Martyrology did appear in 1586 under Sixtus V, which may be where the date comes from. Safe wording: 'left out of the Roman Martyrology when it was drawn up in the 1580s'.

misquoted_or_legend.truth: He was a presbyter (priest), never a bishop. Ingres's 1842 window design labels him 'EPISCOPVS' and the Louvre titles it 'évêque d'Alexandrie', but the ancient sources call him a presbyter.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Jerome, Lives 38; Eusebius 6.11 ('the blessed presbyter'); McGiffert's note to 5.11 ('He was never a bishop'); Louvre INV 20314

misquoted_or_legend.truth: No ancient source says so. Where and when he died is unknown. He was last seen alive carrying Alexander's letter about 211.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Wikipedia infobox (death_place 'Jerusalem', no source); Wace DCB; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He told Christians to give away all their wealth.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The reverse. His sermon on the rich young man says Jesus meant the passions, not the money: 'let no man destroy wealth, rather than the passions of the soul'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, sections 11-14

misquoted_or_legend.claim: His letter about a 'Secret Gospel of Mark' shows what Clement really taught.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The letter is known only from photographs of an 18th-century handwritten copy that Morton Smith said he found at the Mar Saba monastery in 1958. The manuscript is now lost. Scholars still disagree whether it is Clement's, a later forgery or something else.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Geoffrey S. Smith and Brent C. Landau, The Secret Gospel of Mark (Yale University Press, 2023), publisher's description; Wikipedia, 'Clement of Alexandria' ('much debate today over whether it is an authentic letter from Clement, an ancient pseudepigraph, or a modern forgery')
misquoted_or_legend.note: The '18th-century copy' and 'photographs' come from the Wikipedia articles and search summaries, not from a page I read whole. Keep the wording to 'known only from photographs; the manuscript is lost; its origin is disputed'.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He wrote the hymns 'Sunset to sunrise changes now' and 'Jesus, our mighty Lord'.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Both are 20th-century English hymns built on his words: the first a paraphrase by Howard Chandler Robbins (1939), the second by F. Bland Tucker from his Hymn to Christ the Saviour. The Episcopal Church's book calls them 'Clement's writings'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Hymnary.org, 'Sunset to sunrise changes now' (Author: Clement of Alexandria; Paraphraser: Howard Chandler Robbins, 1939) and 'Jesus, Our Mighty Lord' (paraphrase by F. Bland Tucker); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, p. 548
misquoted_or_legend.note: Hymnary pages were read with a fetch tool (curl got HTTP 403); not saved as .txt. The source line in Clement for the first hymn is probably Exhortation 11 ('He hath changed sunset into sunrise'); Hymnary does not say which line.

friends_family_rivals.name: Pantaenus
friends_family_rivals.text: The teacher he 'tracked out concealed in Egypt' and found rest with; Clement succeeded him at the head of the Alexandrian school.
friends_family_rivals.note: Eusebius says Clement names Pantaenus as his teacher in the lost Outlines.

friends_family_rivals.name: Origen
friends_family_rivals.text: Studied under Clement as a boy in Alexandria and later took over the teaching there.
friends_family_rivals.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.6 and 6.3; Jerome, Lives 38
friends_family_rivals.note: The quiz's pair line: 'An early historian says Origen studied under Clement in Alexandria.' Holds.

friends_family_rivals.name: Alexander of Jerusalem
friends_family_rivals.text: His old pupil, a bishop in prison when Clement came to his church; he sent Clement to Antioch with a letter praising him, and later called him 'the holy Clement, my master and benefactor'. Clement dedicated his Ecclesiastical Canon to him.

friends_family_rivals.name: Tatian the Syrian
friends_family_rivals.text: Clement attacks Tatian's teaching that marriage is corruption ('Tatianum arbitror Syrum talia audere dogmata').
friends_family_rivals.source: Stromata, Book 3, chapter 12 (left in Latin in the ANF)
friends_family_rivals.note: Some scholars guess the 'Assyrian' among his six teachers was Tatian; that is only a guess, not in the sources checked.

friends_family_rivals.name: Julius Cassianus
friends_family_rivals.text: An Encratite teacher whose arguments against marriage Clement answers.
friends_family_rivals.source: Stromata, Book 3, chapter 13 ('Julii Cassiani Haeretici Verbis Respondet')

friends_family_rivals.name: Basilides and Valentinus
friends_family_rivals.text: Gnostic teachers of Alexandria whose ideas of martyrdom and death he refutes.
friends_family_rivals.source: Stromata, Book 4, chapters 12 and 13 (chapter titles 'Basilides' Idea of Martyrdom Refuted', 'Valentinian's Vagaries About the Abolition of Death Refuted'); Catholic Encyclopedia: 'Basilides and Valentinus taught there'

friends_family_rivals.name: Carpocrates and Epiphanes
friends_family_rivals.text: Father and son whose sect taught that wives should be held in common; Clement refutes them.
friends_family_rivals.source: Stromata, Book 3, chapter 2 (Latin in the ANF: 'Carpocratis Et Epiphanis Sententiam de Feminarum Communitate')

friends_family_rivals.name: Photius
friends_family_rivals.text: The 9th-century patriarch of Constantinople who listed errors in Clement's lost Outlines but praised the Instructor.

friends_family_rivals.name: Jerome
friends_family_rivals.text: Called him 'in my judgment the most learned of men'.

how_he_died.text: No one recorded it. He was alive about 211 in Cappadocia; by Alexander's letter to Origen (about 215) he was among 'those blessed fathers who have trodden the way before us'. No last words, no grave, no later legend of his death was found.
how_he_died.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.11 and 6.14; McGiffert's note 1878; Catholic Encyclopedia (1908); Wace DCB
how_he_died.note: The page's 'How he died' section can be one short paragraph, or folded into 'Is he a saint?'.

is_he_a_saint.text: It depends on the church, and this is one of the questions people search. Anglicans keep him (5 December). Coptic writers call him St Clement, but he has no day in the Coptic Synaxarium. He is not on the Catholic or Orthodox calendars. The old Western martyrologies had a St Clement on 4 December; he was left out of the Roman Martyrology in the 1580s, and in 1748 Pope Benedict XIV refused to put him back.

benedict_reasons.text: Benedict XIV gave three reasons: the old writers say almost nothing about his life and holiness; there is no trace of public veneration of him; and some of his teaching is 'at least suspect'. He praised Clement's learning and said he meant no slight to him.
benedict_reasons.source: Benedict XIV, Postquam intelleximus (1 July 1748), sections 19-31, printed in the Martyrologium Romanum (1749); Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): 'Clement's life was little known that he had never obtained public cultus in the Church, and that some of his doctrines were, if not erroneous, at least suspect'
benedict_reasons.note: Latin read in OCR: section 26 ('veterum scriptorum silentio de moribus ... ac vita'), 27 ('Nullum monumentum, imo nec ullum quidem vestigium superest cultus'), 28-30 ('doctrinam dubiam saltem suspectamque'). Section 25: 'non ut de Clementis Alexandrini laudibus quidquam detrahamus'. The date 1 July 1748 is from the search summary (Wikipedia, Roman Martyrology); the OCR text I read did not show the date line.

churches.note: Left out of the Roman Martyrology; Benedict XIV declined to add him in 1748. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1908) still calls him 'St. Clement', and Benedict XVI gave a whole catechesis on him (18 April 2007).
Photius's 9th-century criticism is the best-known Eastern verdict. OrthodoxWiki: 'not commemorated as a saint in Eastern Orthodoxy'.
The Coptic Church's own site calls him 'St. Clement'; no day in its Synaxarium.
5 December: the Episcopal Church, ACNA, the Anglican Church of Canada. Not the Church of England.
Not in the LCMS or ELCA calendars.

quote_for_page.exact: Down to the seventeenth century he was venerated as a saint. His name was to be found in the martyrologies, and his feast fell on the fourth of December.
quote_for_page.note: Its next sentence ('dropped from the calendar on the advice of Cardinal Baronius' under Clement VIII) is where it differs from Benedict XIV's own account; see misquoted.

is_he_a_saint.note: Wikipedia also says 'The Eastern Orthodox Church officially stopped any veneration of Clement of Alexandria in the 10th century' (tagged 'citation needed'); no source for it was found. Do not print it.

hub_card.text: Hints hold. Church Father (Jerome calls him 'presbyter of the Alexandrian church'; he is an Ante-Nicene Father). Lived about 150 to 215, so 'pre300'. Greek-speaking, taught at Alexandria, so 'east'.
hub_card.note: Not a martyr, not a monk, not a Cappadocian. 'teachers' (great-teachers) would fit his work as head of the school, if that group means teachers rather than Doctors of the Church; he is not a Doctor of the Church. Leave that to the owner.

could_not_verify: The Coptic Church's own calendar status beyond the copticchurch.net Synaxarium: some Coptic parishes or schools may keep him locally. Wikipedia's 'venerated in Coptic ... Ethiopian Christianity' has no calendar behind it that I found.
Wikipedia's feast '4 December (Eastern Catholicism, Anglicanism)': no Eastern Catholic calendar and no Anglican calendar with 4 December was found (the Anglicans checked all use 5 December).
Wikipedia's 'The Eastern Orthodox Church officially stopped any veneration of Clement of Alexandria in the 10th century' (tagged citation needed): no source found.
OCA and GOARCH calendars were not checked directly for Clement of Alexandria; absence rests on OrthodoxWiki and a saint.gr search.
The current (2004) Roman Martyrology was not opened; the 1916 English edition and Benedict XIV's 1748 bull were.
The exact date of Benedict XIV's bull (1 July 1748) comes from a search summary, not from the page I read.
Epiphanius, Panarion 32.6 was read only through Westcott's quotation in Wace's Dictionary, not in the Panarion itself.
Cassiodorus, Institutions 1.8 was read only as quoted by Benedict XIV (OCR Latin).
Why the Anglican churches chose 5 December rather than the old 4 December: no source.
Hymnary.org pages returned 403 to curl; their credits were read through a fetch tool and are not saved as .txt. F. Bland Tucker's year for 'Jesus, our mighty Lord' was not confirmed.
The Secret Gospel of Mark details (18th-century copy, photographs only) rest on the Yale publisher's page plus Wikipedia summaries, not a scholarly article read whole.

checker_fixes_2026_09_25: Feast days: the Anglican Church of Canada's Book of Common Prayer (1962) keeps him on 4 December (calendar p. xii). The draft said no church keeps 4 December now.
Status line: 'Kept by Anglicans' narrowed to 'Kept by some Anglican churches' (not the Church of England).

Teachers (Stromata 1.1): the draft's retelling ('others in southern Italy and in the East, an Assyrian, and a Hebrew') did not match its own count of six; retold after Wace/Westcott (first an Ionian in Greece, others in Magna Graecia, others in the East, the last in Egypt). The count of six rests on McGiffert (note 1516) and Westcott (Wace: 'six illustrious teachers'); the Catholic Encyclopedia's list implies seven, so the count depends on how the sentence is read.

John and the robber: 'promising young man' is not the source ('a youth, powerful in body, comely in appearance, and ardent'); 'soon' is not the source ('by degrees'); 'the fiercest, the bloodiest, the cruelest' describes him as captain, not the band.
Rich man: 'godless and treacherous' is the opening of the same sermon, not a separate earlier remark ('Then he wrote a whole sermon').

Docetism: 'critics call this close to Docetism' replaced by the source: 'Photius has accused Clement of Docetism' (Catholic Encyclopedia). 'think Him a phantom' replaced by the text's own 'a different opinion of Him'.
Persecution: Stromata 4.10 condemns giving oneself up; it does not simply say 'flee'. Retold as 'should not hand themselves over'.
Gelasian list: 'In the 500s' has no source among those checked (the Catholic Encyclopedia gives no date); removed.
Prayer: the Instructor does not end with the prayer; a hymn follows it (Book 3, chapter 12).

Alexander's book: 'on the Church's canon' could be read as the canon of Scripture; the title is given instead (Ecclesiastical Canon, or Against the Judaizers; McGiffert note 1850 says kanon here means a rule of practice).
Cappadocia and Clement looking after Alexander's church: Eusebius 6.11 does not name Cappadocia as the place of the prison; the Catholic Encyclopedia (after Duchesne) does. Cite added.
Origen as Clement's pupil: 'The 190s' changed to 'Before 202' (Origen was 17 in 202; McGiffert note to 6.6).

Sources: Benedict XIV's letter is read in an 1859 printing of the Roman Martyrology (archive.org bub_gb_pl0AUPENnqoC), not the 1749 one; Hymnary's credit for Tucker's 'Jesus, our mighty Lord' now read (Author Clement of Alexandria c. 200; Paraphraser F. Bland Tucker, 1895-1984) and linked.
